e.t: This word means “sleeplessness”—the condition or experience of being without sleep. It refers to wakefulness when sleep is absent, whether for a short period or through repeated nights. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Corinthians. The word appears in 2 Corinthians 6:5 and 11:27, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain how sleeplessness functions in each passage.

This word means “unchangeable,” describing something that cannot be altered, reversed, or made different. It refers to a settled quality rather than an action: what is unchangeable remains firm and does not shift. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hebrews 6:17–18. The word’s basic sense is therefore one of permanence and stability. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains that the matter being described is fixed and cannot be changed.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to recognize” or “to tell.” It describes recognizing someone or making someone known, depending on how it functions in the sentence. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 7:13. Its precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense concerns recognition or disclosure rather than a general statement or description.

This word means “endless”: something without a stopping point or known limit. It describes what continues on without reaching an end, functioning as a descriptive word rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 1:4. Its basic meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described as endless there.

“Balak” is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Revelation 2:14. Because it is a proper name, its basic meaning is the person designated by the name; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain why Balak is mentioned there. Thus, this word functions as a name, not as a general term.

me: Verb, Present, Either middle or passive, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to force” or “to force one's way.” It describes exerting strong pressure or pressing forward rather than proceeding passively. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 11:12 and Luke 16:16. Its exact emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the central idea remains determined force or vigorous action. The word therefore points to active pressing, compelling movement, or forceful pursuit, rather than merely desiring something or waiting for it to happen.

This word means a finger or fingers, referring to the digits of the hand. It is an ordinary bodily term used for a specific part of the hand, whether one digit or more than one is intended. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times in eight verses, showing a consistent physical meaning rather than an abstract idea. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, which supplies the action or comparison involving the finger.

e.t: This word means to test something carefully and then approve it or regard it as fit. It can describe examining a matter to determine its worth, correctness, or suitability. In the New Testament, it is used 22 times, including contexts involving discerning what is right, evaluating conduct, and examining what proves genuine. Thus, it carries both the testing process and the resulting judgment: something is examined so that what is acceptable may be recognized and approved.

The word refers to a drachma, meaning a silver coin used as money. It names a monetary object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times in two verses, all within Luke. Its basic meaning is specific and straightforward: a coin that could be counted or possessed. The surrounding verse determines the particular significance of that coin in its setting.

This word means “deeply” or “earnestly.” It is an adverb that strengthens the action of a sentence, showing that something is done with exceptional intensity, seriousness, or heartfelt effort rather than casually. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 22:44. Its meaning therefore points to the manner and intensity of an action, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that intensity is expressed there.

This word refers to a precept or rule—a stated instruction intended to direct conduct. It presents guidance as something laid down for people to observe, rather than merely a casual suggestion. The central idea is an established command or regulation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, so its meaning is consistent but its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word refers to a feast or festival—a recognized occasion of communal celebration, often connected with religious observance. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 25 times in 23 verses, naming such appointed celebrations rather than an ordinary meal. It can describe the festival period itself or the public occasion associated with it. The surrounding passage determines which particular feast is meant, but the central idea remains a formally recognized time of celebration and gathering.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to run together,” describing people or things moving toward the same place or converging as a group. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in Mark 9:25. The word focuses on coming together in motion, rather than merely being together after movement has stopped. It is therefore a precise action word for gathering or rushing together, with the surrounding passage determining exactly who or what is moving.

This word means “fit” or “suitable,” describing something appropriate for a purpose or well matched to what is needed. It can describe a person or thing that is properly suited for its intended use. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing twice in Luke and once in Hebrews. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as the purpose or standard of suitability.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “be fruitful” or “to produce a good crop.” It describes successful fruitfulness, especially the result of land or plants yielding a good harvest. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 12:16. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself; its basic meaning remains productive, fruitful yield.

This word means “amazement”—a strong response of astonishment when something remarkable is seen or experienced. It describes a person’s emotional reaction rather than the event itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Luke and Acts, and consistently refers to people being deeply struck by what they witness. The surrounding passage determines what caused the amazement in each occurrence, but the word itself points to an intense sense of wonder or astonishment.

This word means “service”—work performed for the benefit or care of others. It refers to practical activity carried out on someone’s behalf rather than merely an inward attitude or intention. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, so its meaning is concise and focused rather than broadly represented across many passages. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word describes something regarded as precious—highly valued and of equal worth. In the New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Peter 1:1, and its ordinary sense identifies what is valued rather than disregarded. The wording can stress preciousness itself or parity of value: something is “as precious as” something else, or “equally valuable.” The surrounding verse determines what is being compared or honored.

This Greek New Testament word means “and” or “and there.” It connects one statement with another, while in some sentences it points to a place or situation already being discussed. Thus, it may simply continue a thought, or it may join the idea of being there with what follows. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek New Testament, across Matthew, Mark, John, and Acts. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central function is to connect and continue.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to bring” or “to bring down.” It describes moving or leading someone or something from one place to another, with the direction sometimes understood as downward. The word occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, especially in Acts, where it is used for bringing people to a location or bringing them down. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains directed movement from one place to another.

This word means “key” or “keys,” referring to an object used to open or secure something. In the New Testament, it is used six times, both for a single key and for multiple keys. The word can describe an actual key and can also be used in passages where a key represents access or authority to open and close. Its references span Matthew, Luke, and Revelation, with four of its six occurrences in Revelation.

Michael is a personal name rendered “Michael” in the Greek New Testament. It identifies a named figure rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. The name occurs twice in this corpus: once in Jude 1:9 and once in Revelation 12:7. Its basic lexical function is therefore identification—pointing to Michael by name. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain what Michael is doing or how he is presented in either passage.

This word means “house,” referring to a dwelling or household. It is a noun used throughout the Greek New Testament for a physical home and, depending on the sentence, the people or family associated with that home. Its central idea remains a household as a place of residence and belonging. The word occurs 114 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that homes and households are a recurring part of its vocabulary. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word means “wholly” or “through and through,” describing something as complete in every part rather than partial or limited. It emphasizes entirety and full extent. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Its exact force in that verse is best understood from the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning points to something complete throughout. The two glosses together show that the word stresses fullness from one end or aspect to another, not merely a large degree or approximate completeness.

e.t: This word means “from all directions” or “from all sides.” It describes something approaching, surrounding, or extending toward a place from every direction rather than from just one side. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, each in a different verse, showing a consistent sense of complete surrounding or movement from every side. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what is being described, but the central idea remains something coming or present all around. [Citations: Mark 1:45; Luke 19:43; Hebrews 9:4]

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to anger”: to provoke or cause someone to become angry. It describes an action rather than anger as a feeling or state. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, so its basic meaning is clear even though its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its two recorded occurrences are in Romans 10:19 and Ephesians 6:4. In ordinary terms, it points to conduct that stirs anger in another person.

e.t: This word describes threatening someone further—continuing or adding to a threat already made. It is a verb expressing a repeated or intensified act of warning harm or punishment, rather than a general feeling of anger. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 4:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of threatening again or further.

e.t: This word means “to roll before” or “to roll in front of.” It describes the action of moving or positioning something by rolling it ahead of, or in front of, another place or object. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, thing, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew and Mark, with the same basic sense.

e.t: This word means “to suffer together with” or “to suffer with.” It describes sharing in another person’s hardship rather than facing difficulty entirely alone. As a verb, it expresses joining someone in suffering, endurance, or costly service. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Timothy. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains united participation in suffering with another person.

This word describes confusion or uproar—a condition in which order is disturbed and people or circumstances become unsettled. It points to disorder rather than a calm, organized situation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 19:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a state of confusion or tumult. The word’s two closely related meanings emphasize both inner disorder and the outward commotion that can result from it.

e.t: This word means “to join” or “to join together.” It describes the act of bringing people into one united bond rather than leaving them separate. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, showing a consistent sense of being brought together. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is connection and union.

This word means “to associate with”—to have fellowship or company with someone. It describes a person’s connection with others rather than an isolated action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in 1 Corinthians and 2 Thessalonians. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains association or companionship with another person.

This Greek New Testament word means “childbearing,” referring to the bearing or having of children. It names the process itself rather than describing a particular person or event. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Timothy 2:15. That reference identifies its location, but the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain how the term functions in that specific sentence. Its central meaning remains childbearing, and no broader sense is established here.

e.t: This word means “to abound,” “to increase all the more,” or to become especially plentiful. It describes an increase that goes beyond what was already present, emphasizing an overflowing or greatly enlarged amount. In the Greek New Testament, it appears two times, so its meaning is focused and consistent rather than broadly varied. The word is used in Romans 5:20 and 2 Corinthians 7:4, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular force in either passage.

This word means “corruption” or “perishableness”—the condition of decay, ruin, or passing away rather than lasting permanence. It can describe what is subject to deterioration and therefore cannot endure unchanged. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, including passages concerning what perishes in contrast with what is imperishable. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains decay or susceptibility to corruption.

This word means “flight,” referring to the act of fleeing or getting away. It names movement away from a place or situation rather than a person, command, or emotion. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its precise force in Matthew 24:20 must be understood from that verse’s surrounding wording; the word itself supplies the basic idea of flight.

This word refers to a quart, a unit used for measuring dry goods or other commodities. It is a noun naming a quantity rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both within Revelation 6:6. The word itself identifies the measure; the surrounding verse is needed to understand what is being measured and why that quantity matters there.

e.t: This word means “emphatically” or “exceedingly,” intensifying the force of what is being said. It functions as an adverb, showing that an action, statement, or feeling is expressed with especially strong emphasis or to an extraordinary degree. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 14:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central sense is clear: it strengthens the expression rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself.
